title: Ursula K
content: I was six years old. At the time, I was left at home with my younger sister while my mother and another sibling went out. I remember feeling unwell because I was suffering from a cold or flu. In my young mind, I was determined to make myself better. I had always been highly competitive with my older siblings and wanted desperately to prove that I could be just as capable, responsible, and resourceful as they were. Believing that medication would hasten my recovery, I went into the kitchen, opened the medicine cabinet, and began pulling out boxes of tablets and pills. I started ingesting them, one after another, thinking, "Just one more, just one more." I truly believed that the more I took, the quicker I would be well again. Many of the tablets had a sweet, powdery taste, almost like candy, which made it easier to keep trying different ones. Unbeknownst to me, some of these medications were dangerously inappropriate for a child, such as my mother’s heart medication for arrhythmia and my father’s antidepressants. Once I had finished, I calmly returned to the living room. I recall looking at my little sister and saying, almost dreamlike, "Aunt, dear sisters, I’m going on a trip. Please cook lunch for me. We’ll eat when I return." Those were the last words I remember uttering before I lost consciousness. What followed was something I’ve carried with me my entire life. I found myself floating above my body in what I now understand was the operating room. From a corner of the room, I could see myself lying motionless on the table while doctors worked desperately to revive me. They were applying electric shocks to my chest, but the heart monitor remained flat. I was clinically unresponsive. While I hovered in that space, I experienced a profound sense of peace, joy, and unconditional love. It was beautiful, and I didn’t want to return. I felt completely at ease; free, whole, and deeply connected to something greater. Looking down at my small, lifeless body, I felt an overwhelming compassion. It was if I was observing the fate of a dear child that I no longer identified with. I also felt immense empathy for the medical staff working so hard to save me. Then, I became aware of my mother. I saw her weeping in the hospital corridor from being consumed with guilt and anguish. I felt the depth of her pain and sensed the crushing burden of self-blame she would carry if I were to die. It was at that moment, I made the decision to return. I could not bear the thought of her living the rest of her life believing she had caused my death. The next thing I remember is waking up. I was confused, disoriented, and tied to a hospital bed. The restraints were likely put in place for my safety. I had no idea where I was or what had happened. Ever since that day, I have carried with me an unrelenting questions, "Why did I come back? What is my purpose on this planet?" Life has not been easy, and I have often wondered what God or the universe intended for me by sending me back. But one thing has always been clear; that experience changed me. It gave me a deep sense that my life is not arbitrary, and that perhaps I am here to do something meaningful that touches the lives of others. Sadly, I often feel as though my life has been unremarkable. I haven’t achieved anything that the world would consider extraordinary such as a dazzling career, widespread influence, or a visible legacy to inspire the masses. There are no awards, no accolades, no public triumphs to speak of. I experienced a loveless marriage with no children. I feel I am just living my life for my mother and my younger sister. But what I have done is to support my mother throughout her entire life. I’ve been there for her emotionally, logistically, and financially. I was always the one she could rely on, even though I was not her favorite child. I supported her quietly, faithfully, and consistently. Yet still, it was I who stood by her; through illness, hardship, losses, divorce, and the long, painful process of placing her into care when her health deteriorated. When she became seriously ill, I left work and spent an entire year by her side to care for her. Towards the end, I arranged everything which included ultimately her move into a care home. It was one of the most painful chapters of my life. Out of four children, I was the only one who stayed and showed up to visit her. And although she may not have given me the most affection, she gave me her trust. I hold her notarial power of attorney. I am the one she turns to. And yet, there are days I wonder, "Is this my life’s purpose? Was this the reason I came back? To be her guardian, her anchor, her daughter until the end? And if so, when she leaves this world, will my mission here be complete? Will I be free to return to that place of overwhelming peace, joy, and love that I once glimpsed as a child? I can't wait.

elements.At the time of your experience, was ther: No, Accident, Drug or medication overdose, Clinical death (cessation of breathing or heart function)
elements.Did you feel separated from your body?: I clearly left my body and existed outside it
elements.How did your highest level of consciousn: More consciousness and alertness than normal, I was six years old, so my alertness and consciousness level was literally a meter away from the floor. I lived in my little world of dolls and playing house. I felt smart for a six-year-old, but clearly my thinking was flawed and very human. My reasoning, decision-making, and analysis of information available to me at that time in my real life were misinterpreted, fitting the human thinking level and capabilities of a six-year-old child. However, during my out-of-body experience, I could see everything happening at the same time, hear my internal dialogue, and make decisions from a standpoint of peace, love, empathy, and joy, like a wise, experienced, calm, and content person.
elements.At what time during the experience were: Looking at myself from the ceiling, I felt wise, smart, intelligent, well-informed, decisive, at peace, loving. It was almost like I analyzed and used critical thinking in my internal dialogue at superfast speed, although I had no recollection in terms of time. I understood everything happening around me with intense clarity.
elements.Did time seem to speed up or slow down?: Everything seemed to be happening at once; or time stopped or lost all meaning, I have no recollection of time. I don't know if that event took three minutes or three hours. Time didn't matter because it was as if it disappeared.
elements.Please compare your vision during the ex: I can't compare my vision other than to the day of the incident. I saw everything from the perspective of a six-year-old child. During my out-of-body experience, I saw everything from the top down and through the walls. I could see the monitor behind me or next to me, facing the doctors, not me. I could see my mother behind the wall and the doctors while I was up in the ceiling.
elements.Please compare your hearing during the e: When I was at home, I heard everything like a normal human being. During my experience, I could hear everything clearly. But, with a bit more distance as if I was detached from the scene with my sense of hearing.
elements.Did you see, or feel surrounded by, a br: A light clearly of mystical or other-worldly origin
elements.What emotions did you feel during the ex: I felt ever-present love, joy, and peace.
elements.Did you feel a sense of harmony or unity: I felt united or one with the world
elements.Did you suddenly seem to understand ever: Everything about the universe, "Everything" is a big word. However, I understood that love is the answer to everything.
elements.What was your religion prior to your exp: Christian- Catholic, At age six, I didn't have any religious attachment. But, I was raised in a practicing Catholic family.
elements.Have your religious practices changed si: Yes, Not immediately, but at the age of 14, I received a new age self-help book and immediately resonated with its content. Then I got another one and immediately knew that church was a scam, but energy, the universe, spirits, and different dimensions are real. Once more, it brought a lot of peace to my life, and I made many good decisions by being faithful to those teachings.
elements.What is your religion now?: Christian- Catholic, Not really practicing anymore, but still am Catholic.
elements.Did your experience include features con: Content that was entirely not consistent with the beliefs you had at the time of your experience, Prior to my out-of-body experience, I don't remember being very close to my mother. After that experience, she became my world. I cannot say I had beliefs before about God, the universe, or my purpose in this world because I was only six years old. But the distinction between caring for my mom and not doing so is very clear to me.
elements.Did you have a change in your values and: Uncertain, I was too young to remember how I was before the accident, so I can't relate.
elements.During your experience, did you gain inf: Yes, I did not encounter any specific information regarding life's meaning or purpose. I was clear on my mission or purpose in this life because it was my own private mission to help my mom.

Uncertain, I did not receive any specific information; however, I had this feeling that I was going somewhere else. In other words, while I was looking at my lifeless body from the top of the room, I felt at peace. I felt empathy, love, and I felt like it was enough. It was time to pass over and go somewhere else. I was excited about it. I wanted to go, feeling that seconds before I noticed my mother. That's when everything changed, and I decided to come back. That makes me feel like the place I wanted to go was a happy place, somewhere I was looking forward to. That room and being out-of-body was not my destiny.
Yes, Love is the answer to everything.
elements.Have your relationships changed specific: Uncertain, Not with people, just my mother.
elements.Was the experience difficult to express: Uncertain, I was six years old and couldn't articulate it. But, in my mind, it was crystal clear and without a doubt it took place.
elements.How accurately do you remember the exper: I remember the experience more accurately than other life events that occurred around the time of the experience, I don't remember any birthdays, Christmas, or other events that happened that year; or years before or after. But that memory never left me. I remember accidents, such as losing my fingers at age six, overdosing on pills at age seven, being run over by a car at age 14, nearly drowning at 17. However, all these events I remember clearly, but everything in between is hazy. Moments that were nice, but in general, I couldn't recall which year those events took place.
elements.Are there one or several parts of your e: I find comfort in knowing that I will be at peace and loved when I die. Everything will be okay once I die, which makes the hardships of this life easier to swallow. But the sadness of being alive is deeper in me and the longing to return is stronger.
elements.What did you believe about the reality o: Experience was definitely real, I felt like I was crazy. I didn't have anyone to talk to about this, and I didn't trust anyone in my family to ask about what happened to me. But I thought about it a lot for years, asking myself if I was mentally ill or what had happened to me.
elements.What do you believe about the reality of: Experience was definitely real, The first time I heard about the books Life After Life and Life After Death, I rushed to read them. I was astonished to discover that so many people had gone through experiences similar to mine. It was a profound moment of validation and reassured me that I wasn't imagining things, and I certainly wasn't losing my mind. The accounts I read mirrored my own in striking ways, especially the key elements. This brought me a deep sense of reassurance and peace, confirming that what I had experienced was real. One question has always stayed with me: why do some people go through such experiences only once, while others encounter them multiple times? I don't have the answer, but I have never doubted the truth of what I lived through. And throughout my life, one constant has remained: caring for my mother. That has been the thread woven through everything.
